help.intro: The dative is the third case, and the one everyday German leans on most after the accusative. It marks the receiver — the person something is given, shown, told or done to: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch — and it follows a group of verbs (helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, antworten) and a group of prepositions (mit, bei, nach, zu, aus, von, seit). The question is wem? (to whom?). Its articles are the ones you have met as chunks since the start of the course (im, am, beim): der → dem, das → dem, die → der, and the plural → den with an -n added to the noun itself (mit den Kindern). The indefinite article follows: einem, einem, einer; and kein, mein and the other ein-words do the same: meinem Vater, meiner Mutter, meinen Eltern.
help.tips[0].text: Masculine and neuter → dem; feminine → der; plural → den and the noun takes -n (den Kindern, den Freunden — unless the plural already ends in -n or -s: den Frauen, den Autos).
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I give the man, the woman and the child a present.
help.tips[0].trap: English marks the receiver with word order or 'to'. German marks it on the article; the dative 'der' is feminine, not masculine — the same word does two different jobs.
help.tips[0].check.q: Der Lehrer gibt ____ Schülern die Hefte zurück.
help.tips[0].check.why: Schülern is plural (with the extra dative -n), and the dative plural article is always den.
help.tips[0].visual.caption: The new row. In the plural the noun takes an -n too: mit den Kindern.
help.tips[1].title: Ask wem?
help.tips[1].text: Wem gibst du das Buch? – Dem Mann. Wem hilfst du? – Der Frau. If the question is wem?, the answer is dative.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: Whose bag is it? – The (female) teacher's.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: Who are you helping? – The neighbour.
help.tips[1].check.q: Wem schreibst du eine Karte? – ____ Oma.
help.tips[1].check.why: A wem? question wants a dative answer, and die Oma becomes der Oma in the dative.
help.tips[2].title: Verbs that always take the dative
help.tips[2].text: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, antworten, gratulieren, schmecken, passen, fehlen. The person after them is dative, with no accusative at all.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: The guest likes the cake. The dress fits the woman.
help.tips[2].check.why: gehören always takes the dative, and das becomes dem.
help.tips[3].text: The ein-words take -em, -er, -em and -en: einem Mann, einer Frau, einem Kind, meinen Eltern. No dative plural of ein; kein and mein do have one: keinen Kindern, meinen Freunden.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: I help a friend. He thanks his father.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: We are giving our children a game.
help.tips[3].check.why: gratulieren takes the dative, and the ein-words add -em for a masculine noun: meinem Bruder.
help.remember[0]: dem–der–dem–den: say it as a four-beat chant, and add -n to the plural noun.
help.remember[1]: wer? nominative, wen? accusative, wem? dative.
help.vocab[3].en: to please (+ Dativ) — X gefällt mir = I like X
help.context.en: Today my neighbour has her birthday. I congratulate the neighbour and give her flowers. The neighbour likes the flowers a lot. Her husband thanks me and shows the visitors the garden. Then he helps the children with the bike. A nice day at the neighbours'!
help.mistakes[2].why: The receiver is dative: feminine der.
help.hook: Give, help, thank, congratulate: learn dem, der and den, and German finally tells you who receives what.
help.table.caption: The articles in three cases
sentences[0].english: I give the book to the man.
sentences[0].why: The receiver of geben is dative: der → dem Mann.
sentences[1].why: helfen always takes the dative: die → der Frau.
sentences[2].why: danken takes the dative: das → dem Kind.
sentences[3].why: mit always takes the dative; the plural article there is den, and the noun adds -n too.
sentences[4].english: The car belongs to the teacher.
sentences[4].why: gehören takes the dative: der → dem Lehrer.
sentences[5].why: The one given to is dative: die → der Katze.
sentences[6].english: I give the father a tie.
sentences[6].why: schenken: the receiver is dative — der → dem Vater; the tie stays accusative.
sentences[7].why: antworten takes the dative: die → der Lehrerin — you answer TO someone.
sentences[8].why: helfen + dative, plural: den Nachbarn — dative plural always ends in -n.
sentences[9].english: The bike belongs to the girl.
sentences[10].english: She tells the children a story.
sentences[10].why: The listeners are dative: den Kindern — article den and noun -n, the plural's double n.
sentences[11].english: The waiter brings the guest the bill.
sentences[11].why: The one brought to is dative: der → dem Gast.
sentences[12].english: I show the tourist the way.
sentences[12].why: zeigen: the person shown to is dative — die → der Touristin.
sentences[13].english: The child likes the ice cream.
sentences[13].why: schmecken works on the dative: dem Kind — it tastes good TO the child.
sentences[15].english: The shoes don't fit the boy.
sentences[15].why: passen takes the dative: dem — and Junge is a weak noun, adding -n itself: dem Jungen.
sentences[16].english: We wish Grandma a happy birthday.
sentences[16].why: gratulieren takes the dative: die → der Oma — you congratulate TO someone in German.
sentences[17].why: helfen + dative plural: den Patienten — den plus the plural -n.
